query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Ni or Co into a primarily BCC refractory high-entropy alloy will create a minor ductile FCC sub-phase that significantly increases overall ductility and uniform deformability, while preserving the high strength and maintaining impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline refractory BCC-based high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbMoTaW-based or similar), which exhibits desirable strength and energetic performance but limited ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled Ni (or Co) addition (e.g., 5–10 at.%) during vacuum arc melting and apply forging/thermal treatments to stabilize a BCC + FCC dual-phase microstructure.
generation.conditions: Alloy melts prepared under inert atmosphere, cast via vacuum arc melting, then subjected to forging and moderate-temperature heat treatment (e.g., 1000–1200 °C). Mechanical tests (tensile and dynamic strain-rate) conducted at ambient or slightly elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: A minor fraction of ductile FCC sub-phase distributed within the BCC matrix to accommodate more uniform plastic deformation.
generation.mechanism: The FCC sub-phase enhances dislocation slip and partial twinning capability, delaying crack initiation and propagation to improve ductility without significantly diminishing the underlying matrix strength or energy release behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped BCC baseline, the Ni/Co-substituted alloys should display notably higher tensile ductility (e.g., a moderate boost in uniform elongation) with minimal strength trade-off and similar energetic performance under dynamic loading.
generation.baseline: The reference BCC refractory HEA, known for high strength and moderate energy release but poor ductility during deformation.
generation.boundary: If Ni or Co exceeds ~15 at.% or the dual-phase distribution is not well controlled, additional embrittling phases (e.g., intermetallic compounds) may form, offsetting ductility gains or diminishing energetic properties.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence suggests dual-phase strategies improve ductility, the optimal Ni/Co content and precise phase fraction remain uncertain and require systematic experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce a series of vacuum arc-melted alloys with 0%, 5%, 10%, and 15% Ni (or Co) additions to a BCC-based refractory HEA, followed by forging and uniform heat treatment to form dual-phase microstructures. Evaluate mechanical response via tensile and dynamic impact tests.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation at quasi-static and high strain rates
Quantitative phase analysis (XRD, SEM/TEM) to confirm FCC volume fraction and microstructure
Impact energy release via drop-weight or split-Hopkinson pressure bar tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni/Co additions do not yield improved uniform ductility or significantly compromise strength/energy release (>15% drop) compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: Taking into account the effect of strain rate, Li et al. conducted tensile simulations on an AlCrFeCuNi alloy and a CoNiFeAlCu alloy to study the mechanical properties of the alloys and the main mechanism of plastic deformation. The results showed that the AlCrFeCuNi alloy had not only high strength but also good plasticity. With the increase in strain, the AlCrFeCuNi alloy produced dislocation and stratification. Dislocation slip twins were the main deformation mechanism of the AlCrFeCuNi high-entropy alloy. Due to severe lattice distortion and high local strain, the CoNiFeAlCu alloy induced a phase transition from FCC to BCC. This phase transition mechanism can make the CoNiFeAlCu alloy obtain high ductility and high strength at the same time. In addition, this phase transition is mainly affected by the strain rate [,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community. HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in that they have at least four principal elements, instead of one or two in the latter. It is a breakthrough to the alloy design in the traditional physical metallurgy, and it opens a new arena for explorations of new materials and new properties. Previous studies have indicated that HEAs have a high softening resistance at elevated temperatures, and sluggish diffusion kinetics. Therefore, HEAs are widely regarded as highly promising high-temperature materials. Before the high-temperature application of HEAs can be seriously pursued, a technical challenge in terms of the mechanical property needs to be tackled. Basically, single-phased HEAs have been found difficult to reach a reasonable balance between strength and (tensile) ductility. Single-phased fcc structured HEAs are ductile but not strong enough. Single-phased bcc structured HEAs, on the other hand, can be very strong but at the price of brittleness. chosen.why: Adding Ni (or Co) is a direct and well-known route to stabilize ductile phases and reduce the base alloy’s brittle-to-ductile transition temperature. The creation of a dual-phase matrix (e.g., BCC + FCC) can accommodate plastic deformation more uniformly, thus improving ductility without sacrificing the underlying high strength or the capacity for impact-induced energetic response. Standard vacuum arc-melting, subsequent forging, and heat treatments are straightforward methods for tuning the microstructure, making this a plausible research direction that addresses the question’s need for increased ductility and uniform deformability while preserving performance.
